title: Your values
hook: what matters most to you, in five words? the prophet Micah's courtroom answers in three (Micah 6:1-8)
tomorrow: why would the rabbis say: do good, even for the wrong reason?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: written down. Franklin's black spots, the Sikh rahit, the Buddhist precepts, each a way of life put on paper. But what goes on the paper first?

The courtroom is outdoors. In the book of the prophet Micah, God calls his people to trial, and the mountains and hills are the jury. Then God speaks, and it isn't an accusation. It sounds hurt: "O my people, what have I done unto thee?" The people scramble for an answer. What should we bring? Burnt offerings? Calves? Thousands of rams? Ten thousand rivers of oil? Our firstborn children? Every offer gets bigger and more desperate. And then the prophet gives the verdict.
screen: `THE MOUNTAINS ARE THE JURY.` → `O MY PEOPLE, WHAT HAVE I DONE?` → `RAMS? RIVERS OF OIL?` → `THE VERDICT.`

segments.voice: "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" Three things, and none of them is an offering. The whole bidding war of rams and oil was answering a question nobody asked. The word translated mercy is the Hebrew chesed: loyal, steady kindness, the love that keeps showing up. Here's the teaching, held by Jews and Christians who read Micah as scripture. In the Hebrew prophets, what God wants isn't a bigger gift. It's a way of living: fair dealing with others, kindness that doesn't quit, and humility before God. Micah fits the whole ask into one breath. That's the challenge in today's line. What matters most to you, in five words? Not what would look good on a list. Notice what the people in the story did. They went for the expensive answer, the one that cost the most and showed the most. The verdict was quieter and harder. Justice, mercy and humility are things you do on a Tuesday with the people in front of you. So the test of a value isn't how grand it sounds. It's whether you'd recognize it in an ordinary afternoon. Micah's three are verbs: do, love, walk.
screen: `DO JUSTLY, LOVE MERCY, WALK HUMBLY.` · `CHESED: KINDNESS THAT KEEPS SHOWING UP.` · `NOT A BIGGER GIFT: A WAY OF LIVING.` · `VALUES YOU'D SEE ON A TUESDAY.` · then, large: `FIVE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Say five words that matter most to you out loud, one per breath, slowly. Then say them again, and with each one, call up a recent ordinary moment where you saw it, or missed it.
Your values: what matters most, small enough to say in one breath, like Micah's do justly, love mercy, walk humbly.
Take this one: five words. Micah needed three, and every one was a verb. That's day 1590.

screen: `DAY 1590 COUNTS.` → `FOUNDATIONS · 4 OF 10.` → `TOMORROW: WHY WOULD THE RABBIS SAY: DO GOOD, EVEN FOR THE WRONG REASON?`

howItsDone: Jews read Micah among the prophets, and Christians read it in the Old Testament; there, 6:8 stands as the prophet's own summary of what the LORD requires.
